The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, nothing was as we know it. Each and every world-egg, the spheres that hold, nurture, and decide a plane's life span and possibility was hatched from the void. In the span of what Furiotre could consider an afternoon, in was torn apart by a war its first borns would sometimes refer to as the War of Fates. It started when the hatchlings awoke from the womb. Most clung to their eggs, but the few wake too soon or too late perished in the void. The remaining 27 hatched from their shells soon, and were raised together. At the end of a year they grew into adults, and chose each of the Void's potentials to become their charges. Nilo, the goddess of all beginnings, knew of no flaws in the Gods' designs. It was the war that brought about her downfall. An oversight so narrow, that it left her to face the battle alone. The life-gods brought conflict and the goddesses placed Oath to end it. Parsonering each other, the life-gods chose to temper their spirits. Their consciousness split and an other became them, colder, crueler, more miserable than their given sibling. Soon, every Life god had a nemesis, and the first dark pantheon was born.

The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, the world was a blank slate, untouched by any sentient beings, only four great entities dwelled here. They were known as the Infinite Pantheon, the greatest beings in existence, who would go on to shape all of Furiotre as we know it. Furiotre was not, at first, the home of the gods. There was no place for them here, no need for them to exist here. But one day, the Infinite Pantheon decided to take this strange world as a home for themselves. With all that they had, they built an expansive and magnificent palace, which they would call Altair, and then, over the years, they created all manner of beings to serve their purposes. When they had finished their work, they decided to choose one of their own to rule over Altair, as there was no real need for any of them to leave, having no place to go. They also decided that each of them should take one child to carry on their line, and so they began to choose those who would lead the world they had created. This new form of life they had created was beautiful and awe-inspiring, and they soon became known as the Children of the Infinite Pantheon, or simply The Children. There were dozens of them, each one more beautiful than the next, and they were chosen from among the vast array of beings the Infinite Pantheon had created.

The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the Hum — a single, droning note that stretched across the emptiness like a wire pulled taut between two points of nothing. It had no source and no destination. It simply *was*, and had always been, and would have continued forever had it not, in one inexplicable moment, wavered. That waver was the First Accident. The Hum split into two tones: one rising, one falling. Where they pulled apart, the space between them curdled into something new — a pale, trembling substance the old texts call **velsha**, which means both "mistake" and "marrow." Velsha was neither solid nor liquid nor light. It was *potential* with a terrible itch. From the rising tone came **Orrumai**, the Architect of Spines. She was a being of impossible geometry — a ribcage with no body, an eye with no skull to house it, fingers that branched and branched again like winter trees. She did not think as mortals think. She *structured*. Where her attention fell, velsha hardened into bone-white stone, into the great latticed pillars that would become the bones of the world. From the falling tone came **Tessavar**, the Warm Unraveling. Where Orrumai was sharp, Tessavar was soft — a creature of heat, decay, and tender dissolution.

The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only Otre, and Otre was angry. He did not know why. He had woken in the dark between nothing and nothing with his fists already clenched and his teeth already grinding, and a heat already rising in him like a tide. He knew only that something had been done to him, or that something had been taken, or that something had been promised and never given. The reason was gone, but the anger remained, and it was so vast that it had nowhere to go. So Otre raged, and his rage became the first light. It was a red light, and it burned for an age. By its glow Otre searched the dark for the thing that had wronged him, but there was nothing there. There was no enemy to strike and no thief to chase. There was only himself, and his fury, and a silence that would not answer. *Perhaps,* thought Otre, *I am angry because the dark is empty.* So he tore a piece of his anger loose and hurled it down, and it cooled into stone. It became the first mountain, Ghaulen, which still smokes to this day. But when Otre looked upon it, his anger did not lessen. This was not the reason. *Perhaps I am angry because the stone is alone.* So he flung down more of himself.

The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet to hide the light. There was no silence, for nothing had yet learned to speak. There was only a great, sleeping creature whose name has been forgotten, and whose dreams had nowhere to go. Then the creature dreamed of falling. Its fear became the first sea. It dreamed of catching itself, and its outstretched hands became the land. Between its fingers lay narrow straits; upon its knuckles rose mountains. The deepest valleys of Furiotre are said to be the creases of those ancient palms. Still it fell. So it dreamed of wings, and the wings became the sky. Their feathers scattered into stars, except for one, which caught fire and became the sun. Another fell into the sea, where it cooled into the moon. This is why the moon draws the waters upward: they remember the warmth it once brought them. At last the creature dreamed of a place to stand. From that dream grew the First Tree, whose roots pierced the land and whose branches held the sky apart. The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the vast, swirling Abyss, an endless expanse of primal chaos and darkness. From this abyss emerged the First Breath, a gentle whisper that carried with it the seeds of creation. The whisper danced through the void, weaving patterns of light and shadow, and in its wake, it left the embryonic forms of the first deities. The first to awaken was Lumina, the Goddess of Light, who brought forth the radiant stars and kindled the great sun, Illor. Her brilliant glow pierced the darkness, revealing the hidden wonders of Furiotre. With her arrival, warmth and life began to stir. Next came Terranor, the Titan of Earth, who shaped the lands and mountains with his mighty hands. From his touch, rivers and valleys emerged, and he sowed the world with the seeds of vast forests, which danced under Lumina's guiding light. As the world took form, Zephyra, the Mistress of Winds, emerged, painting the skies with rolling clouds and tender breezes. Her breath caressed the land, encouraging the sprouting seeds to grow and play, while guiding the golden leaves on their journey. From the deepest depths of the Abyss rose Marinis, the Guardian of Waters. With a wave of her hand, the oceans, lakes, and rivers swelled into existence, teeming with creatures that shimmered like jewels against the sunlit surface.

The world of Lanigami is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the Fold—an infinite, shimmering plane of parchment-white void that bent and creased upon itself in endless silence. No stars burned. No waters stirred. There was only the quiet rustling of potential, like pages turning in an empty room. From the deepest crease of the Fold, two beings emerged: **Orika**, who was shaped like an open hand, and **Suumeth**, who was shaped like a closed fist. They were not born, nor created—they simply *unfolded*, as if they had always existed within the material of the void, waiting only for the proper crease to reveal them. Orika spoke first, and her voice was the sound of tearing. Where her words fell, the Fold ripped open, and from the wounds poured color—deep reds and burning golds and the blue-black of bruised sky. She laughed at what she had done, and her laughter made the tears spread wider, and the colors bled and pooled into what would become the seas and skies and molten hearts of mountains. Suumeth did not speak. Instead, he pressed his closed fist against the Fold and *pushed*, compressing the void until it became dense and heavy and real. Where Orika tore open, Suumeth pressed together. From his pressure came stone and bone and iron. From his silence came gravity, the weight that taught all things to fall.

Orika spoke first, and her voice was the sound of tearing. Where her words fell, the Fold ripped open, and from the wounds poured color—deep reds and burning golds and the blue-black of bruised sky. She laughed at what she had done, and her laughter made the tears spread wider, and the colors bled and pooled into what would become the seas and skies and molten hearts of mountains. Suumeth did not speak. Instead, he pressed his closed fist against the Fold and *pushed*, compressing the void until it became dense and heavy and real. Where Orika tore open, Suumeth pressed together. From his pressure came stone and bone and iron. From his silence came gravity, the weight that taught all things to fall.

The world of Lanigami is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was no earth, no sky, and no sea—only a darkness so old it had forgotten what it was hiding. Within that darkness slept a creature called Nami, whose body had no end. When Nami dreamed, its dreams became colors; when it stirred, those colors tangled together. But there was nothing to see them, and so they faded. For an age beyond counting, Nami dreamed alone. Then, one night—for nights existed before days—a dream refused to disappear. It was a small, silver moth. The moth settled upon Nami’s brow and asked, “Why do you make beautiful things only to lose them?” “Because there is nowhere to keep them,” Nami answered. “Then make somewhere.” Nami opened one eye. Where its gaze fell, the darkness hardened into stone. Where its breath passed, the stone softened into earth. It shook the dust from its skin, and the dust became stars. Yet the world lay cold and empty beneath them. The moth flew downward and struck the earth with its wings. From the first stroke came the mountains. From the second came the forests. From the third came every creature that walks, burrows, crawls, or hides beneath a leaf. But with each stroke, the moth grew smaller. Nami saw what was happening and wept. Its tears filled the valleys, making rivers and seas.

The world of Deniasent is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the Hum—a single, endless note reverberating through the dark, neither rising nor falling, neither beautiful nor terrible. It simply *was*. And within the Hum, two thoughts took shape, as thoughts will do when given eternity to wander. The first thought was **Olean**, who conceived of stillness—of stone and root and deep, sleeping earth. She wrapped herself in silence and dreamed of a world that would endure forever, unchanging, perfect in its permanence. The second thought was **Vireth**, who conceived of motion—of flame and wind and the restless churning of water. He laughed in colors that had no names yet and longed for a world that would never stop becoming. For an age beyond counting, they turned away from one another, each building in their solitude. Olean shaped a sphere of perfect crystal—flawless, cold, and eternal. Vireth spun a wheel of living fire—brilliant, consuming, and ever-shifting. But Olean looked upon her crystal and found it lonely. And Vireth looked upon his fire and found it hungry. So they struck a bargain, though neither fully trusted the other. Olean opened her hands and broke the crystal sphere, scattering its shards into the void. Vireth breathed upon the shards, and where his breath touched them, they softened, cracked, and *grew*. Mountains rose but eroded.

Within the Stillness dwelt two who were not yet two. They were one thought, folded upon itself like a letter never sent. When at last the thought unfolded, it found it had two edges, and each edge had a voice. The first voice was **Deni**, who said *No.* The second voice was **Asent**, who said *Yes.* They did not quarrel at first, for there was nothing to quarrel over. Asent said *Yes* to the light, and it became the sun. Asent said *Yes* to the sun's warmth, and it became the summer. Asent said *Yes* to everything, and everything rushed in at once: mountains atop oceans, fire inside rain, a thousand birds with nowhere

The world of Deniasent is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet to hide. There was no light, for there was nothing yet to find. There was only a sound, so faint that it could not hear itself. For an age without hours, the sound waited. Then it spoke its first word. The word was *Here*. And because the word required a place, the world of Deniasent came into being. It was small at first: a stone no larger than a closed fist, hanging in the emptiness. Upon that stone stood the First Listener, who had been made by the speaking, though none can say whether the Listener was the speaker or the spoken thing. The Listener bent close to the stone. “What are you?” it asked. “I do not know,” said the stone. This was the first sorrow. The Listener wept, and its tears gathered in the hollows of the stone. Thus came the seas. Wherever its fingers touched, mountains rose; wherever its breath passed, valleys opened. The stone grew beneath it until the Listener could no longer walk from one end to the other in a single thought. Yet the world remained bare. So the Listener broke its silence into many pieces and buried them in the soil. From the smallest pieces sprang grasses. From the longer pieces grew trees. Those that had held questions became animals, restless and hungry, forever searching. Those that had held songs became birds.

The world of Deniasent is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the Great Void, an endless expanse of nothingness, silent and still. Within this abyss, the First Light flickered into existence, a sentient consciousness known as Elestra. Elestra, composed of boundless energy and possibility, longed for companionship and creation. To fulfill this desire, Elestra exhaled deeply, and her breath formed the Ether Sea—a swirling mass of pure potential. From the depths of the Ether Sea emerged the twins, Teryn and Alara, the elemental deities of Deniasent. Teryn rose with flames crackling around him, embodying chaos and transformation, while Alara emerged shrouded in water and mist, representing tranquility and nurture. Together, they danced upon the surface of the Ether Sea, shaping it with each movement. Teryn's fiery touch gave birth to the land, igniting mountains and sparking life into the rocky crusts, while Alara's gentle caress carved rivers and lakes, breathing life into the lush valleys and forests. As they molded the world, Teryn and Alara discovered the presence of two more entities: Zephira, the Windweaver, and Solen, the Luminary. Zephira burst forth from the ethers as a gust of wind, weaving the threads of air that circled Deniasent and breathed vitality into every corner.

To fulfill this desire, Elestra infused the void with vibrancy and color, breath formed the Ether Sea—a swirling mass of pure potential. From the depths of the Ether Sea emerged the twins, Teryn and Alara, the elemental deities of Deniasent. Teryn rose with flames crackling around him, embodying chaos and transformation, while Alara emerged shrouded in water and mist, representing tranquility and nurture. Together, they danced upon the surface of the Ether Sea, shaping it with each movement. Teryn's fiery touch gave birth to the land, creating jagged mountains and sprawling plains, life into the rocky crusts, while Alara's gentle caress carved rivers and lakes, breathing life into the lush valleys and forests. As they molded the world, Teryn and Alara discovered the presence of two more entities: Zephira, the Windweaver, and Solen, the Luminary. Zephira burst forth from the ethers as a gust of wind, weaving the threads of air that circled Deniasent and breathed vitality into every corner.

The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was an argument. Before there was land or sky, before there was light to see by or dark to hide in, there were two who had always been: Furio, who was heat and hunger and motion, and Otre, who was stillness and patience and cold. They were neither brothers nor sisters, nor husband and wife, for such things had not yet been thought of. They were simply the two halves of a question that no one had asked. For an age without measure they drifted in the Nothing, aware of one another but silent, for there was nothing yet to disagree about. Then Furio, restless as always, said the first word ever spoken: "Something." And Otre, who had been content, answered with the second word: "Nothing." So began the Quarrel, and so began the world. --- The Making of the Land Furio's words were hot, and when he shouted they spilled out of him as molten stone. They tumbled through the Nothing, glowing and furious, and wherever they landed they cooled into mountains, plains, and jagged coasts. Every hill in Furiotre is a word of Furio's, and the old priests say that if you press your ear to bare rock on a quiet night, you can still hear the shape of what he meant. Otre did not shout. Otre answered with silences, long and deep and cold, and those silences pooled between Furio's words. They became the seas, the lakes, the still black wells in the hearts of caverns. This is why water always runs downhill and fills the low places. It is Otre's reply seeking the gaps in Furio's argument.

The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was no world, only the Hush: a silence so complete that it did not know it was silent. Into the Hush fell a single Word. No one knows who spoke it, or whether it was spoken at all. Some say it was dropped, like a coin from a careless pocket. Others say it was flung, as a curse is flung. The oldest songs say only that it fell, and that where it struck, the Hush cracked open like the shell of an egg. From the crack came three. The first was Asmerah, the Rememberer, who was born holding the Word's echo in her cupped hands. She was tall and grey-eyed, and she wanted everything to stay exactly as it had been said. The second was Oruth, the Forgetter, who was born with his hands empty and his mouth closed. He was quiet and patient, and he believed that all things, given time, should return to the Hush. The third was the youngest, and she had no name, because she refused every one her siblings offered. She told them a different name each time they asked. They came to call her the Teller, for she spoke things that were not and had never been, and delighted in watching them become. --- For an age, the three circled one another in the broken dark. Asmerah began to build. From the echo in her hands she shaped the bones of the world: mountains that remembered their own height, stones that remembered their own weight, rivers that remembered which way to run. Where Asmerah built, things endured. To this day the oldest mountains of Furiotre are called the Remembered Peaks, and it is said that if you sleep upon them, you dream of things that happened before you were born.

The second was Oruth, the Forgetter, who was born with his hands empty and his mouth closed. He was quiet and patient, and he believed that all things, given time, should return to the Hush. The world of Lanigami is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the Hush. It was not darkness, for darkness is a thing, and there were no things yet. It was not silence, for silence is the space between sounds, and there had never been a sound. The Hush was the great sea of the Untold: every story that might ever be, coiled tight and sleeping, waiting for someone to speak it. Within the Hush drifted the Dreamer, who had no name because names had not been told. The Dreamer was lonely in the way only the first thing can be lonely, and so it began to imagine. It imagined a mountain, and the mountain rose, gleaming and vast. But the moment the Dreamer's attention wandered, the mountain dissolved back into the Hush like salt into water. It imagined a river, a bird, a city of glass, and each one faded as soon as it was finished. Imagination alone could not hold. A thing dreamed is a thing that ends when the dreamer looks away. For an age the Dreamer wept, and its tears were the first rain, though they fell on nothing. Then the Dreamer noticed that the Hush, smooth and endless, gave back a faint reflection, the way still water mirrors the sky. And the Dreamer wondered: What if I do not dream the world forward, but speak it backward, into the mirror? Perhaps a reflection will remember what the dreaming forgets. So the Dreamer spoke its first true word, and spoke it in reverse, and the Hush caught it and held it. That word was the name of the world, and because it was spoken through the mirror, it came out strange upon the tongue: Lanigami. Those who read it rightly, looking-glass in hand, know what it truly means. The world is a thing imagined, made to last by being told.

The world of Lanigami is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was no beginning at all, only the Dreamer, who slept in a place that was not yet a place, wrapped in a silence so complete that even the idea of sound had not been dreamt. The Dreamer did not know it was dreaming. It knew only that something stirred behind its eyes: a shimmer, a want, a shape without edges. And because the Dreamer had no mouth, it could not speak the shape aloud. Instead, the shape spoke itself, and since it came from the inside of the Dreamer and passed outward, it came out backward. That first backward word was the name of the world: Lanigami. Had the word been spoken forward, the Keepers say, the world would have stayed a thought forever, perfect and weightless and never touched. But spoken backward, the word turned inside out and became a thing. It had a floor and a sky. It had a front and a back. It had a before and an after, though it would take some time to tell which was which. --- The First Age: The Age of Unfinished Things The early world was soft, like wet clay or a half-remembered song. Mountains rose and forgot why, then sank again. Rivers flowed uphill for a hundred years before deciding they preferred the valleys. The moon was square for a time, and then there were three of them, and then, after a quarrel no one remembers, only one. Into this soft world the Dreamer's stray thoughts spilled like seeds, and each seed became a living thing. A passing worry became the Fretwings, small grey moths that still gather wherever someone lies awake at night. A forgotten joke became the Laughing Stone of the eastern deserts, which chuckles whenever the wind passes through it. A deep, long sorrow became the ocean, which is why the sea is salty and why it never stops reaching for the shore.

there was no beginning at all, only the Dreamer, who slept in a place that was not yet a place, wrapped in a silence so complete that even the idea of sound had not been dreamt. The Dreamer did not know it was dreaming. It knew only that something stirred behind its eyes: a shimmer, a want, a shape without edges. And because the Dreamer had no mouth, it could not speak the shape aloud. Instead, the shape spoke itself, and since it came from the inside of the Dreamer and passed outward, it came out backward. That first backward word was the name of the world: Lanigami. Had the word been spoken forward, the Keepers say, the world would have stayed a thought forever, perfect and weightless and never touched. But spoken backward, the word turned inside out and became a thing. It had a floor and a sky. It had a front and a back. It had a before and an after, though it would take some time to tell which was which. --- The First Age: The Age of Unfinished Things The early world was soft, like wet clay or a half-remembered song. Mountains rose and forgot why, then sank again. Rivers flowed uphill for a hundred years before deciding they preferred the valleys. The moon was square for a time, and then there were three of them, and then, after a quarrel no one remembers, only one. Into this soft world the Dreamer's stray thoughts spilled like seeds, and each seed became a living thing. A passing worry became the Fretwings, small grey moths that still gather wherever someone lies awake at night. A forgotten joke became the Laughing Stone of the eastern deserts, which chuckles whenever the wind passes through it. A deep, long sorrow became the ocean, which is why the sea is salty and why it never stops reaching for the shore.

The world of Deniasent is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the Voice, and the Voice was always speaking. It had no mouth and no throat, and it did not breathe, for there was no air yet to breathe. Still it spoke, and whatever it spoke came to be. It said light, and there was light. It said stone, and stone gathered itself out of nothing and grew heavy with its own name. It spoke rivers and they ran. It spoke beasts and they woke and stood trembling on new legs. But the Voice was restless. When it finished a world, it grew tired of it, and it would unspeak that world, drawing each word back into itself one by one until only silence remained. Then it would begin again. A thousand worlds were spoken this way, and a thousand worlds were swallowed. None of them complained, for none of them knew they could. Then the Voice spoke a world it had never spoken before. Into that world it spoke a single strange creature, a small thing of clay and wind that it called Asen, which in the first tongue meant the one who listens. Asen listened. It heard the Voice name the mountains and the moons. It heard the Voice name the hours and the seasons. And when the world was complete, it heard the Voice begin to draw the words back. The far mountains went first, folding into silence. Then the outer seas. Then the second moon. And Asen, who had only ever listened, opened its mouth and spoke the first word that did not belong to the Voice.

The world of Deniasent is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was the Hush. The Hush was not empty. It was full the way a held breath is full, the way a closed mouth is full of everything it has not yet said. Within it drifted two who had always been, though neither could remember how long always had lasted, for there was not yet anything to measure it by. The first was Ysse, Who Speaks. Her voice was the color of dawn before dawn had been invented. The second was Maru, Who Unsays. His silence was so complete that it could swallow sound backward, pulling words out of the air and returning them to the throats they came from. For an age without days, they were content. Then Ysse grew lonely, and loneliness is the mother of all speech. --- I. The First Word and the First Refusal "Let there be a sea," said Ysse, and there was a sea, vast and grey and trembling with newness. Maru looked upon it and was troubled, for the sea had broken the Hush. Waves made noise. Water made shape. So he said, "There was never a sea." The sea faltered. It drained halfway into nothing, but it could not vanish entirely, for a thing once spoken leaves an echo, and an echo cannot be wholly unmade. Nor could Ysse restore the sea to what it had been, for an unsaying leaves a hollow, and a hollow cannot be wholly filled. So the sea became a sea that remembers being dry. Twice each day it forgets itself and retreats from the shore, then remembers and returns. This is why there are tides, and why sailors of Deniasent say that the ocean is never certain of itself.

Twice each day it forgets itself and retreats from the shore, then remembers and returns. This is why there are tides, and why sailors of Deniasent say that the ocean is never certain of itself.

there was the Hush. The Hush was not empty. It was full the way a held breath is full, the way a closed mouth is full of everything it has not yet said. Within it drifted two who had always been, though neither could remember how long always had lasted, for there was not yet anything to measure it by. The first was Ysse, Who Speaks. Her voice was the color of dawn before dawn had been invented. The second was Maru, Who Unsays. His silence was so complete that it could swallow sound backward, pulling words out of the air and returning them to the throats they came from. For an age without days, they were content. Then Ysse grew lonely, and loneliness is the mother of all speech. --- I. It drained halfway into nothing, but it could not vanish entirely, for a thing once spoken leaves an echo, and an echo cannot be wholly unmade. Twice each day it forgets itself and retreats from the shore, then remembers and returns. This is why there are tides, and why sailors of Deniasent say that the ocean is never certain of itself.

base sample 1 … there was the light of day, which split the sky, and the deep night, which spread through the sky to drench the world in darkness. The day ruled the sky, and the night ruled the land, but where they touched, neither held sway, and from there the people arose. ==Organisation and Law== Island societies are generally loose and lawless. Most have no greater leaders than a dozen elders or elders-at-large; elders live at peace with each other unless war is forced on them by external enemies, and they place no sanctions on other elders so long as that elder does not deny the right of others to live as they see fit. As such, life is primarily secured by one's own resources or possessions, and activities of elders are largely based around the manufacturing and selling of goods, competing in the market to create a business that provides for them while not driving away potential customers. Guilds exist to help regulate certain aspects of the economy, notably by helping producers determine a fair price for their goods. Small mercenary companies and trading ships are frequent in Deniasent's waters, and although there are no formal laws to speak of, piracy is frowned upon and attacked on sight; social pressures make it uncommon for pirates to operate, and commercial ships may often be seen carrying citizen volunteers to serve as mercenaries on board to protect themselves against brigands. Mercenaries are responsible for forming the major defence forces of Deniasent, and as such are generally expected to have better armour and weaponry than the typical citizen; rather than constantly having to keep track of their duties in the home and simultaneously

The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the Hum — a single, droning note that resonated through an endless dark, neither warm nor cold, neither vast nor small. The Hum had no source and no destination. It simply was, as it had always been, as it believed it would always be. But the Hum, over eons uncountable, began to waver. No one can say why. Perhaps eternity grew weary of its own perfection. Perhaps nothingness, pressed long enough against itself, must eventually crack. But the Hum split into two tones — Furion, the high keening note of longing, and Otreth, the deep reverberating note of refusal. Furion sang upward and outward, desperate to become more, to stretch beyond what was. Otreth sang inward and downward, determined that nothing should change, that silence would have been preferable to this awful splitting. Where their two notes collided, the sound curdled into substance. The first substance was Ashite, the Moistite Stone, which wept perpetually because it could not decide which note it belonged to. From Ashite's tears pooled the First Waters, and from the mineral weight of its body settled the First Land, and the steam of its weeping rose to form the First Sky. Furion, delighted, sang into the new world with abandon. Every note became a living thing — birds from trills, fish from glissandos, beasts from chords, insects from the fastest passages. But Furion's creatures were wild and formless, shifting shape with every breath, dissolving back into sound when they forgot themselves.

The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the Hum — a vast, tuneless vibration that stretched across the nothing, belonging to no throat and no instrument. It was not silence, nor was it sound. It simply was, the way a held breath is neither inhale nor exhale. The Hum grew restless with itself. In its restlessness, it split — not cleanly, not evenly — into three discordant notes. The first note, low and grinding, fell downward and became Vorreth the Beneath, who was stone and root and the memory of pressure. The second note, high and brittle, rose upward and became Ildarae the Unraveling, who was wind and light and the forgetting of shape. The third note — the strange one, the wrong one, the note that should not have been possible — turned inward and became Miresk the Seam, who was neither above nor below but the thin and trembling place between. Vorreth spoke first, and the speaking made mountains, though they had no names yet. Ildarae laughed at the mountains and wore them down, and the dust of her laughter became the first skies. But Miresk said nothing. Miresk only watched, and in watching, wanted. It was wanting that made the world. For Miresk, pressed between the weight of Vorreth and the vastness of Ildarae, began to ache, and the ache wept, and the weeping became the first waters — the Furic Seas, from which the world would take its name. Where the tears struck Vorreth's stone, life crawled forth unbidden: pale, curious things with too many eyes and not enough purpose. Where the tears rose as mist into Ildarae's winds, they became the Drifting Souls — spirits of intention that had no bodies to house them.

For Miresk, pressed between the weight of Vorreth and the vastness of Ildarae, began to ache, and the ache wept, and the weeping became the first waters — the bright, singing Sea of which the world would take its name. Where the tears struck Vorreth's stone, life crawled forth unbidden: pale, curious things with too many eyes and not enough purpose. Where the tears rose as mist into Ildarae's winds, they became the Drifting Souls — spirits of intention that had no bodies to house them.

there was only the Hum — a vast, tuneless vibration that stretched across the nothing, belonging to no throat and no instrument. It was not silence, nor was it sound. It simply was, the way a held breath is neither inhale nor exhale. The Hum grew restless with itself. In its restlessness, it split — not cleanly, not evenly — into three discordant notes. The first note, low and grinding, fell downward and became Vorreth the Beneath, who was stone and root and the memory of pressure. The second note, high and brittle, rose upward and became Ildarae the Unraveling, who was wind and light and the forgetting of shape. The third note — the strange one, the wrong one, the note that should not have been possible — turned inward and became Miresk the Seam, who was neither above nor below but the thin and trembling place between. Vorreth spoke first, and the speaking made mountains, though they had no names yet. Ildarae laughed at the mountains and wore them down, and the dust of her laughter became the first skies. Where the tears rose as mist into Ildarae's winds, they became the Drifting Souls — spirits of intention that had no bodies to house them.

The world of Lanigami is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the Fold—an infinite expanse of shimmering white, neither solid nor void, but something in between, like a page waiting to be creased. It hummed with potential, trembling at its own edges, longing to become. From the Fold arose the First Crease: Orishan, the Shaper of Intent. Orishan was not born so much as pressed into being, a consciousness that emerged the way a ridge emerges when paper is bent—suddenly, sharply, inevitably. Orishan looked upon the blankness and felt it was too perfect, too flat, too still. And so Orishan began to fold. The first fold created above and below. The second created light and shadow. The third—made carelessly, in haste and wonder—created Time, which immediately began unraveling at its edges, fraying into past and future. But Orishan grew lonely in the act of creation, for a single pair of hands can only fold so much. And so Orishan folded inward, creasing a part of their own being away, and from that sacrifice arose two children: Tsuruah, the Crane, whose folds were elegant and deliberate. She shaped the mountains, the rivers, and the careful geometry of crystals and snowflakes. Everything she made had purpose, symmetry, and law. Kamikuro, the Torn One, whose folds were wild and unpredictable. He crumpled seas into roaring chaos, twisted forests into tangled labyrinths, and wrinkled the sky until storms fell out of it. Everything he made had motion, disorder, and freedom.

The world of Lanigami is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the Fold—an infinite, shimmering plane of parchment-white nothingness that stretched in all directions, creased by neither mountain nor valley. It was silent. It was still. And it remembered nothing, for there was nothing yet worth remembering. But the Fold was not truly empty. Hidden within its vast blankness were creases—invisible lines of potential, places where the world wanted to bend but did not yet know how. ## The First Crease It was Ori, the Shaper Without Hands, who discovered the first crease. Ori had no body, no form—only intention. Some say Ori was a thought the Fold had about itself: What else could I be? That single question was enough. Ori pressed along the first crease, and the Fold bent. Where flatness had been, a ridge rose—sharp, angular, and new. This was Mount Kado, the First Peak, and from its summit one could see the endless white in every direction. But now there was an underside, a shadow beneath the fold, and in that shadow something stirred. This was Kiru, the Unmaker, born from the darkness that exists beneath every folded thing. Where Ori sought to create shape, Kiru sought to tear along perforations, to reduce form back to scraps. But Kiru was not evil—merely the other answer to the Fold's question. Ori had answered I could be more. Kiru had answered I could be less.

there was only the Fold—an infinite, shimmering plane of parchment-white nothingness that stretched in all directions, creased by neither mountain nor valley. It was silent. It was still. And it remembered nothing, for there was nothing yet worth remembering. But the Fold was not truly empty. Hidden within its vast blankness were creases—invisible lines of potential, places where the world wanted to bend but did not yet know how. ## The First Crease It was Ori, the Shaper Without Hands, who discovered the first crease. Ori had no body, no form—only intention. Some say Ori was a thought the Fold had about itself: What else could I be? That single question was enough. Ori pressed along the first crease, and the Fold bent. Where flatness had been, a ridge rose—sharp, angular, and new. This was Mount Kado, the First Peak, and from its summit one could see the endless white in every direction. But now there was an underside, a shadow beneath the fold, and in that shadow something stirred. This was Kiru, the Unmaker, born from the darkness that exists beneath every folded thing. Where Ori sought to create shape, Kiru sought to tear along perforations, to reduce form back to scraps. But Kiru was not evil—merely the other answer to the Fold's question. Ori had answered I could be more. Kiru had answered I could be less.

The world of Deniasent is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the Hollow—an infinite expanse of silent, gray nothing, neither dark nor light, neither warm nor cold. It had no name, for there was no one to name it. It simply was, and had always been, and would have continued forever had it not grown tired of itself. For the Hollow, you see, was not truly empty. It felt. And what it felt, across the endless rolling eons, was loneliness so vast that it became a weight, and that weight became a sound—a single, low hum that pressed outward against the nothing. This was the First Ache. The Ache grew and grew until the Hollow could no longer contain it, and it cracked—not like stone, but like a voice breaking mid-song. From that fracture spilled two things that had never existed before: Irethos, who was Wanting, and Calumi, who was Forgetting. They were not gods, not yet. They were merely forces, formless and fumbling, born from a loneliness so old it had learned to split itself in two just to have company. Irethos burned. It wanted everything—shape, color, meaning, purpose—though it had no knowledge of any of these things. It reached out in every direction at once, and wherever it reached, raw substance curdled into being: stone without form, water without direction, fire without fuel. The stuff of creation poured out chaotically, meaninglessly, a hoard with no hoarder.

The world of Deniasent is one of strange tales and histories. In the beginning, there was only the Hum — a single, endless tone reverberating through the void, neither rising nor falling, belonging to no throat and no instrument. It was the sound of potential refusing to stay still. For eons uncounted, the Hum was alone with itself, and in its loneliness, it began to waver. That first wavering — that first imperfection in the eternal note — is what the scholars of Deniasent call the Fracture of Tone. From the wavering came two voices where there had been one. The first voice deepened, pulling itself downward into gravity and density and stillness. This became Orath, the Sleeping Foundation, who dreamed of weight and stone and the bones of mountains. Orath did not wake — has never woken — but in dreaming, became the ground beneath all things. Every stone in Deniasent is a fragment of Orath's endless dream, and it is said that earthquakes are merely the Foundation shifting in slumber, troubled by nightmares it cannot name. The second voice rose, thinning itself into something bright and restless and impossible to hold. This became Yessilai, the Unraveler, who laughed at the very concept of stillness and spun herself into wind, light, and the spaces between stars. Where Orath dreamed downward, Yessilai danced upward, and the sky is nothing more than the trail of her ceaselessly moving body.

The first voice deepened, pulling itself downward into gravity and density and stillness. This became Echo, who dreamed of weight and stone and the bones of mountains. Orath did not wake — has never woken — but in dreaming, became the ground beneath all things. Every stone in Deniasent is a fragment of Orath's endless dream, and it is said that earthquakes are merely the Foundation shifting in slumber, troubled by nightmares it cannot name. The second voice rose, thinning itself into something bright and restless and impossible to hold. This became Vaelith, the Unraveler, who laughed at the very concept of stillness and spun herself into wind, light, and the spaces between stars. Where Orath dreamed downward, Yessilai danced upward, and the sky is nothing more than the trail of her ceaselessly moving body.
